yevamot-15a-15-15.note: When the daughter-in-law of Shammai the Elder gave birth, Shammai removed part of the ceiling plaster and put branch covering over the bed, as if making a sukka (the booth used on the Sukkot festival) for the newborn. This was raised as proof that Shammai's school really acted on its own rulings. The Gemara answers that onlookers would simply think he wanted fresh air, so it proves nothing.

people.name: Mar Zutra
people.about: raises the objection

terms.meaning: A temporary booth with a leafy roof, in which people eat and sit during the festival of Sukkot.
The school of Shammai, which often disagreed with the school of Hillel.

yevamot-15a-15-15.why: The Gemara is asking whether Beit Shammai actually put their rulings into practice where they differed from Beit Hillel. This incident is offered as evidence that they did, and the Gemara deflects it.

yevamot-15b-1-4.note: Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok saw his teacher, Rabbi Yoḥanan the Ḥorani, eating only dry bread and salt in a drought year. He brought olives, but the teacher politely refused them, fearing they were damp and so ritually impure. Elazar's father explained that the olive barrel had a hole that later got clogged, so the olives were not made susceptible to impurity. The passage ends by noting the teacher always followed Beit Hillel, and concludes that Beit Shammai did generally act on their own rulings.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok
people.about: tells the story

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan the Ḥorani
people.about: a disciple of Beit Shammai

terms.meaning: A status that makes food or objects unfit for certain holy uses until purified; liquids on food can make it susceptible.
A teaching from the time of the Mishnah that was not included in the Mishnah itself.

yevamot-15b-1-4.why: The Gemara is gathering evidence on whether Beit Shammai acted on their own rulings. It argues that praising Rabbi Yohanan for following Beit Hillel makes sense only if Shammai's disciples normally followed Shammai.

yevamot-16a-2-11.note: The Sages heard that Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas, who was very old and nearly blind, had ruled that a certain woman was permitted. A group (Rabbis Yehoshua, Elazar ben Azarya and Akiva) visited him, and he said the law follows Beit Hillel; the other ruling, he explained, came from his sharp younger brother Yonatan. Leaving by three doors, they looked for Yonatan, and Akiva met him and answered all his objections. Yonatan then insulted Akiva, who replied modestly that he had not reached even the level of shepherds.

people.name: Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas
people.about: very old, nearly blind and wealthy

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
people.about: a great Sage though young

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: also called Akiva ben Yosef

people.name: Yonatan ben Harkinas
people.about: Dosa's younger brother and a disciple of Shammai

terms.meaning: A law case about whether the co-wife of a man's daughter is permitted to his brothers for levirate marriage, which Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel disputed.
The school of Hillel, which often disagreed with the school of Shammai.

yevamot-16a-2-11.why: The Gemara had quoted only the opening line, as evidence that Beit Shammai's view was once followed in practice; here it tells the whole incident. Afterward it explains Haggai's other two rulings.

yevamot-21b-1-2.note: Rav Hisda recalled hearing from a great man, Rabbi Ami, that the Sages forbade a daughter-in-law only because of a daughter-in-law, and not understanding it. Chaldean astrologers had told him he would be a teacher. He said to himself: if I become a great teacher, I will work it out on my own; if I become a teacher of children, I will ask the Sages who come to the synagogue. Now, he said, he had worked it out himself: a man's daughter's daughter-in-law was forbidden only because she could be confused with his son's daughter-in-law.
yevamot-21b-1-2.why: The Gemara is listing relatives forbidden by the Sages rather than by the Torah, and has just corrected one item on Rav's list to read his daughter's daughter-in-law. Rav Hisda's account supplies the reason for that prohibition.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Tells how he came to understand a teaching he heard from Rabbi Ami.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: The great man whose short teaching Rav Hisda heard.

terms.meaning: Astrologers who foretold a person's future; here they predict Rav Hisda will become a teacher.
Relatives one may not marry. Some are forbidden by the Torah; the Sages added others so that people would not confuse them with the Torah's cases.

yevamot-25b-4-4.note: An armed bandit being led out for execution told bystanders to tell the wife of Shimon the Priest that he had killed her husband near Lod, and the court allowed her to remarry on that basis. This was brought as proof that a murderer's own statement is accepted. Rabbi Yehuda rejected the proof: the bandit had said only that he was with the murderers, not that he did the killing himself.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: rejects the proof

people.name: Shimon the Priest
people.about: the murdered husband

terms.meaning: A teaching from the time of the Mishnah that was not included in the Mishnah itself.

yevamot-25b-4-4.why: The mishna lets a woman remarry on a witness who says I killed him, while Rabbi Yehuda accepts only we killed him, which Rav Yehuda reads as I was with his murderers. This teaching is the basis for that distinction; the Gemara then explains how a mere accomplice was executed.

yevamot-34b-6-6.note: Ravin brought Rabbi Yohanan's teaching that a woman who waits ten years after her husband before marrying again can no longer bear children; Rav Nahman said this applies only if she did not intend to remarry. Rava told his wife, the daughter of Rav Hisda, that the Sages were gossiping about her, since, as the translation explains, she had borne him children after more than ten years without a husband. She answered: My mind was on you.
yevamot-34b-6-6.why: The Gemara has been discussing sexual relations that cannot lead to pregnancy; it moves to this teaching about when a woman can still conceive, and Rava's exchange shows Rav Nahman's limit on it.

people.name: Ravin
people.about: Brings Rabbi Yohanan's teaching from the Land of Israel.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: The Sage whose teaching about ten years Ravin reports.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: Limits the teaching to a woman who did not intend to remarry.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Tells his wife that the Sages are gossiping about her.

people.name: daughter of Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Rava's wife, who answers that her mind was on him.

yevamot-34b-7-7.note: A woman came to Rav Yosef and said she had waited ten years after her husband's death and still gave birth. Rav Yosef told her not to cast doubt on the Sages' statement. She then confessed that she had had intercourse with a non-Jew during those ten years.
yevamot-34b-7-7.why: Rabbi Yohanan has taught that a woman who waits ten years after her husband before remarrying can no longer conceive. The woman's case looks like a challenge to that teaching, and her confession shows it is not one.

yevamot-37b-5-8.note: When Rav came to Dardeshir, he publicly announced: Who will be my wife for the day? Rav Nahman made the same announcement when he came to Shakhnetziv. The Gemara answers that Sages are different, since their names are famous and their children will always be known. It also explains how they could marry on arrival: they sent messengers ahead so the woman could count seven clean days, or else they only spent time alone with her, since, as the saying goes, one who has bread in his basket is not like one who has none.
yevamot-37b-5-8.why: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov has just taught that a man should not marry wives in two countries, lest his children meet and unknowingly marry each other. The Gemara cites these two Sages' conduct as a challenge to that teaching.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage who, visiting Dardeshir, announced he was seeking a wife for his stay.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: A Sage who did the same when visiting Shakhnetziv.

terms.meaning: After possible menstrual bleeding, a woman counts seven days without bleeding and immerses in a ritual bath before marital relations are permitted.
Being alone together with a woman. Here the Gemara suggests the Sages married only for companionship, not relations.

yevamot-45a-3-3.note: Rabbi Aḥa and Rabbi Tanḥum ransomed captives from Armon and brought them to Tiberias. One woman had become pregnant by a non-Jew, and they asked Rabbi Ami what the child's status would be. He answered that Rabbi Yoḥanan, Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Ḥanina all say that the child of a non-Jew or slave and a Jewish woman is a mamzer.

people.name: Rabbi Tanḥum
people.about: son of Rabbi Ḥiyya

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: gave the answer

terms.meaning: A person born from certain forbidden unions, who is not allowed to marry into the wider Jewish community (a few narrow exceptions apply).

yevamot-45a-3-3.why: The Gemara is debating the status of a child born to a Jewish woman and a gentile or slave. Rav Yosef then answers that counting names proves nothing, and lists Sages who rule such a child of unflawed lineage.

yevamot-45a-11-15.note: A man asked Rav about the status of a child of a non-Jew or slave and a Jewish woman, and Rav said the child's lineage is unflawed. The man, who was such a child, asked to marry Rav's daughter, but Rav refused, and Rav's grandson pointed out that this seemed to contradict his own ruling. Rav said he refused for other reasons, but the man kept pleading and would not leave. In the end Rav fixed his eyes on him and the man died.

people.name: Shimi bar Ḥiyya
people.about: Rav's grandson

terms.meaning: A small measure of grain or produce.

yevamot-45a-11-15.why: Abaye has argued that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi permits such a child to marry within Israel. The Gemara brings this incident to show Rav ruled the same way, then lists other Sages who did too.

yevamot-46a-2-2.note: A convert named Beloreya had slaves who immersed in the ritual bath for conversion before she did. The case came before the Sages, who ruled that the slaves had acquired themselves and become free. Rav Ḥisda used this to raise a difficulty: it seems that had they immersed after her, they would not have become free. This conflicts with an earlier explanation in the Gemara.

people.name: Beloreya
people.about: a female convert

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: raises the objection

terms.meaning: A teaching from the time of the Mishnah that was not included in the Mishnah itself.
Dipping in a ritual bath, a required step in conversion and in freeing a slave owned by a non-Jew.

yevamot-46a-2-2.why: Rav has ruled that a slave bought from a gentile who immerses for conversion before his new Jewish owner immerses him goes free. Rav Hisda infers from this case that had they immersed after her they would not have gone free, and raises it as a challenge; Rava answers it.

yevamot-46a-9-9.note: When Rav Ashi wanted his slave Minyamin immersed, he handed him to Ravina and Rav Aḥa son of Rava, warning that he would hold them responsible. They put a bridle on his neck, loosened it at the moment of immersion and tightened it again at once; the Gemara explains this let the water reach him and kept him from declaring first that he was immersing to become a free man. As he lifted his head from the water they put a bucket of clay on it and told him: Go, take this to your master's house.
yevamot-46a-9-9.why: Shmuel has just said that to stop a slave from declaring his immersion is for freedom, the owner must hold him tightly in the water; this incident shows how that was done.

people.name: Minyamin
people.about: Rav Ashi's slave, who is to be immersed

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Minyamin's master

people.name: Ravina
people.about: One of the two Sages who carry out the immersion

people.name: Rav Aḥa son of Rava
people.about: The other Sage who carries out the immersion

terms.meaning: Dipping in a ritual pool; a slave immersed for slavery joins a Jewish household as a slave, but if he immerses for freedom it makes him a free Jew.
Anything between the body and the water, which makes a ritual immersion invalid.

yevamot-46a-13-14.note: Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba visited Gavla and saw several things that troubled the rules: women pregnant by men who were circumcised but had not yet immersed to finish converting, wine being poured by non-Jews, and lupines cooked by non-Jews that Jews were eating. He said nothing there, but reported it to Rabbi Yoḥanan. Rabbi Yoḥanan told him to announce publicly that the children were mamzerim and the wine and lupines forbidden, being strict because the townspeople were not learned and might otherwise slip into real violations.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba
people.about: visited Gavla

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: told him what to announce

terms.meaning: A person born from certain forbidden unions, who is not allowed to marry into the wider Jewish community (a few narrow exceptions apply).
Dipping in a ritual bath, a required step in conversion.

yevamot-46a-13-14.why: The Gemara has been discussing immersion as the step that completes a conversion. Afterward it shows Rabbi Yohanan's ruling follows his own views: no one is a convert until circumcised and immersed, and a gentile's child with a Jewish woman is a mamzer.

yevamot-46b-13-13.note: Rabba told of an incident in the house of Rabbi Hiyya bar Rabbi. In Rav Yosef's version Rabbi Oshaya bar Rabbi was also there, and in Rav Safra's version Rabbi Oshaya son of Rabbi Hiyya as well. A convert came who had been circumcised but not yet immersed, and he was told: stay here until tomorrow, and we will immerse you.
yevamot-46b-13-13.why: The Gemara has been debating whether circumcision or immersion completes a conversion. Rabba then draws three rules from this incident: a conversion needs a court of three, it needs both circumcision and immersion, and a convert is not immersed at night.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Reports the incident and draws rules from it.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Rabbi
people.about: In whose house the convert came.

people.name: Rabbi Oshaya bar Rabbi
people.about: Present, in the version Rav Yosef teaches.

people.name: Rabbi Oshaya, son of Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: Also present, in the version Rav Safra teaches.

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: Teaches the version with three Sages present.

terms.meaning: A person joining the Jewish people. For a man this requires circumcision and immersion in a ritual bath.
Dip fully in a ritual bath, the final step of conversion.

yevamot-47a-7-7.note: A man known as Jewish told Rabbi Yehuda that he had actually converted in private, so he was not truly Jewish. Rabbi Yehuda asked if he had witnesses, and he did not, and he had children. Rabbi Yehuda ruled that he is believed about himself, so he is barred from marrying a Jewish woman, but he is not believed in a way that would make his children unfit.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: the judge in the case

yevamot-47a-7-7.why: Rabbi Yehuda has just ruled that a conversion done in private, without a court, is not valid. The Gemara then asks how his ruling here fits his other teaching that a father is believed about his children's status, and offers two explanations.

yevamot-48b-12-12.note: Three Sages, Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi, Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha, were sitting in Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha's courtyard and talking. They recalled a city in the Land of Israel whose slaves refused to be circumcised. The masters put up with them for twelve months and then sold them to gentiles. The Sages asked whose opinion the townspeople had followed; the story itself does not give the answer.
yevamot-48b-12-12.why: The discussion is about when a Jewish master may keep an uncircumcised slave. The Gemara answers the Sages' question with a teaching that a master may wait up to twelve months before selling such a slave to gentiles.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina bar Pappi
people.about: One of the three Sages talking in the courtyard.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: One of the three Sages talking in the courtyard.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa
people.about: One of the three Sages; the conversation takes place in his courtyard.

terms.meaning: The Land of Israel.
Non-Jews.

yevamot-59b-6-6.note: Rav Dimi reported from Eretz Yisrael that a girl in the village of Hitlu was sweeping her house when a hunting dog sexually violated her from behind. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi ruled she was still permitted to marry a priest, because she was not considered a zona (a woman disqualified from marrying a priest). Shmuel added that she was even fit for a High Priest, since she was still considered a virgin, and the Gemara clarifies he meant she would be fit for one.

people.name: Rav Dimi
people.about: brought the report from Eretz Yisrael

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: gave the ruling

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: added that she is even fit for a High Priest

terms.meaning: A woman who has had a forbidden relationship and is therefore not allowed to marry a priest.

yevamot-59b-6-6.why: Rabbi Shimi bar Hiyya has just ruled that a woman who had intercourse with an animal is not considered a harlot and may marry a priest; this case is the precedent. The Gemara then asks for the verse showing there is no harlotry with an animal.

yevamot-60b-14-14.note: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi told of a city in the Land of Israel where a family's lineage was challenged. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi sent Rabbi Romanus to investigate. He found that the family included a woman who had converted before she was three years and a day old and had married a priest, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi ruled she was permitted to the priesthood. When Rabbi Zeira asked whether he had drawn his ruling from this case, Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi said he had heard it from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi explicitly.
yevamot-60b-14-14.why: Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi had reported that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules like Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai, who permits a girl converted before age three to marry a priest. Rabbi Zeira wanted to know whether this was said outright or only inferred from this case.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: The Sage who reported the case.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who sent an investigator and permitted the woman to the priesthood.

people.name: Rabbi Romanus
people.about: The Sage sent to examine the family's lineage.

people.name: Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi
people.about: Transmitted Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's ruling and insists he heard it directly.

terms.meaning: The age below which, in Talmudic law, intercourse does not count as removing a girl's virginity. A girl converted before then could be treated as never having had relations as a gentile.

yevamot-60b-18-18.note: A priest married a woman who had converted before the age of three years and a day. Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak asked him why he was breaking the law, and the priest answered that Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi quoted Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi as ruling like Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai, who allows it. Rav Naḥman told him to divorce her, or he would remove Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi from his ear, meaning he would act so the priest could no longer rely on that opinion.

people.name: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak
people.about: objected to the marriage

people.name: Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi
people.about: the source the priest cites

terms.meaning: A descendant of Aaron, who is subject to stricter marriage rules.

yevamot-60b-18-18.why: The Gemara has just shown that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules like Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai on such a convert marrying a priest. This case shows a Sage refusing to rely on that ruling in practice.

yevamot-61a-5-7.note: Yehoshua ben Gamla, a priest, betrothed Marta bat Baitos, a widow. The king then appointed him High Priest, and he went ahead and married her. Rav Yosef saw a conspiracy in the wording that the king appointed him, and cited Rav Asi: Marta bat Baitos brought King Yannai a vessel full of dinars until he made Yehoshua ben Gamla High Priest.
yevamot-61a-5-7.why: The mishna rules that a priest who betrothed a widow and was then appointed High Priest may still marry her, and cites this marriage as the example. The Gemara then reads the wording closely and finds that the appointment was bought.

people.name: Yehoshua ben Gamla
people.about: A priest who betrothed a widow and was then made High Priest.

people.name: Marta bat Baitos
people.about: The widow he betrothed; Rav Asi says she paid the king to appoint him.

people.name: King Yannai
people.about: The king who made Yehoshua ben Gamla High Priest.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: A Sage who saw a conspiracy behind the appointment.

people.name: Rav Asi
people.about: The Sage who reported the payment to the king.

terms.meaning: The first stage of Jewish marriage, which already makes the couple legally bound; the wedding itself comes later.
The chief priest of the Temple. The Torah forbids him to marry a widow.
The brother of a man who died childless; he is obligated to marry the widow (levirate marriage) or release her.
A measure of volume, half a se'a, used here for the size of a vessel full of coins.

yevamot-62b-9-10.note: Rabbi Akiva had twelve thousand pairs of students who all died in one period because they did not treat each other with respect, and the world was left empty of Torah. Rabbi Akiva then taught five new students in the South: Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei, Rabbi Shimon, and Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua, who carried the Torah forward. The Gemara adds that the twelve thousand pairs died between Passover and Shavuot, of what is called a bad death, which Rav Nahman says was diphtheria.

terms.meaning: The holiday, seven weeks after Passover, marking the giving of the Torah.

yevamot-62b-9-10.why: The Gemara is discussing whether a man who already has children should have more. Rabbi Yehoshua reads a verse from Ecclesiastes to say yes, and Rabbi Akiva reads the same verse about students, which his own life illustrates.

yevamot-63a-6-6.note: Rabbi Elazar taught that all craftsmen will one day work the land, and that no occupation is lowlier than farming. Seeing a field that had been plowed across its width, he said to the field that even if it were plowed lengthwise as well, doing business was better than farming it.
yevamot-63a-6-6.why: The Gemara is stringing together sayings of Rabbi Elazar; this one leads into more sayings comparing trade with farming, from Rav, Rava and Rav Pappa.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: A Sage who speaks to a plowed field about how little farming pays.

yevamot-63a-11-12.note: Rabbi Chiyya wished Rav to be saved from something worse than death, and Rav found the verse about a woman more bitter than death. Rav's wife did the opposite of whatever he asked, such as cooking peas when he wanted lentils. When their son Chiyya grew up, he reversed Rav's requests when passing them on, so Rav got what he wanted. Rav praised the idea but told his son not to do it, since it means saying something untrue.

people.name: Rav
people.about: returned from Eretz Yisrael to Babylonia

people.name: Rabbi Chiyya
people.about: Rav's uncle and teacher

people.name: Chiyya
people.about: Rav's son

terms.meaning: The Land of Israel.

yevamot-63a-11-12.why: The Gemara is collecting sayings and stories about wives, good and bad; this one is followed by Rabbi Hiyya's own troubled marriage and more teachings on a bad wife.

yevamot-63a-13-13.note: Rabbi Chiyya's wife constantly aggravated him, yet he brought her gifts. He told Rav it is enough that wives raise the children and keep their husbands from sin, so they deserve thanks. Then Rav Yehuda, teaching his son Rav Yitzchak the verse about a woman more bitter than death, said it described the son's own mother. The Gemara notes that when he taught that a man finds peace only with his first wife, he again named the son's mother as the example. It resolves this: she was sharp but easily calmed.

people.name: Rav Yitzchak
people.about: Rav Yehuda's son

terms.meaning: A teaching from the time of the Mishnah that was not included in it.

yevamot-63a-13-13.why: The Gemara is gathering stories and sayings about wives, and goes on to define a bad wife and what a husband may do about one.

yevamot-64b-10-10.note: Rabbi Yochanan reported that in Tzippori, three sisters each circumcised a son and each baby died. The fourth sister asked Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who told her not to circumcise her son. The Gemara learns from this that he held a pattern becomes an established presumption only after it happens three times.

people.name: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba
people.about: passed on the report

people.name: Rabbi Yochanan
people.about: source of the report

people.name: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
people.about: gave the ruling

terms.meaning: A legal assumption that something will happen again, based on past repetition.

yevamot-64b-10-10.why: The Gemara is asking whether, for Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, a pattern is set by two events or three. This case seems to show three, but the Gemara replies that the third sister may simply never have asked him, and that the case teaches that sisters together can set a pattern.

yevamot-64b-13-13.note: Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef reported an incident before Rabbi Yochanan in the synagogue of Maon, on a Yom Kippur that fell on Shabbat. Two sisters had each circumcised a son who then died. When the third sister came, Rabbi Yochanan told her to go ahead and circumcise her son, because a presumption of danger is not established after only two cases. This is cited as evidence that, in Rabbi Yochanan's view, a presumption is not established after only two occurrences.

people.name: Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef
people.about: came from Eretz Yisrael and reported the incident

people.name: Rabbi Yochanan
people.about: gave the ruling

terms.meaning: A legal assumption that something will happen again, based on past repetition.
The Land of Israel.

yevamot-64b-13-13.why: The Gemara asks what the final ruling is: does a pattern of deaths start after two cases or three? This report is its answer, three. Abaye warns Rav Yitzhak to be sure of his report, since it permits something forbidden and dangerous.

yevamot-64b-15-15.note: Relying on the ruling that a presumption needs three cases, Abaye married Chuma, whose first two husbands had both died. He did not worry that she was a woman whose husbands die. Abaye died while married to her as well.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: married Chuma

people.name: Chuma
people.about: daughter of Isi; her first two husbands had died

people.name: Rachava of Pumbedita
people.about: her first husband, who died

people.name: Rav Yitzchak, son of Rabba bar bar Chana
people.about: her second husband, who died

yevamot-64b-15-15.why: Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef had reported that a pattern is set only after three cases, so a woman widowed twice could remarry. Rava then criticizes Abaye: he himself had called that reporter unreliable, and a rule about circumcision need not apply to marriage.

yevamot-65b-15-17.note: A woman came before Rav Nahman wanting a divorce because her husband could not father children. He told her she was not commanded to have children. She asked whether a woman like her does not need a staff for her hand and a hoe for her burial, and Rav Nahman said that in such a case the husband is forced to divorce her. Separately, Rabbi Hiyya's wife Yehudit suffered terribly giving birth to twins. In disguise she asked him whether a woman is commanded to have children; he said no, and she drank a potion to make herself infertile. When he found out, he said he wished she had borne him one more set of twins, since their sons Yehuda and Hizkiyya and daughters Pazi and Tavi were twins.
yevamot-65b-15-17.why: The Gemara is asking whether a woman is commanded to have children, which decides whether she can demand a divorce from a husband who cannot father them. Both stories assume she is not, and the Gemara next tests that with a case that seems to show the opposite.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: A Sage who forced a husband to divorce his wife so she could have children to care for her.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: A Sage whose wife asked him, in disguise, whether women must have children.

people.name: Yehudit
people.about: Rabbi Hiyya's wife, who drank an infertility potion after painful births.

people.name: Yehuda and Ḥizkiyya
people.about: Rabbi Hiyya's twin sons.

people.name: Pazi and Tavi
people.about: Rabbi Hiyya's twin daughters.

terms.meaning: The commandment to have children. The Sages here hold that it falls on men, not women.
The ketuba, which sets the money a wife receives if she is divorced or widowed.

yevamot-66a-1-1.note: A woman who was half-slave and half-free could marry neither a slave nor a Jew. Her master was forced to free her completely. The Gemara cites this to prove that women are commanded to have children, since presumably she was freed so she could marry and have them. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak rejects the proof: the court forced her release because, unable to marry, she was behaving immorally, and freeing her saved her and others from sin.

people.name: Rav Acha bar Rav Ketina
people.about: passed on the report

people.name: Rabbi Yitzchak
people.about: source of the report

people.name: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak
people.about: offered the second reason

terms.meaning: A non-Jewish slave owned by a Jew, who had a different legal status from a Jew.
To free a slave.

yevamot-66a-1-1.why: The Gemara had said women are not commanded to have children. This case seems to show they are, since her master was forced to free her so she could marry; Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak answers that she was freed to stop the sexual misconduct.

yevamot-66b-7-8.note: A woman brought a fine wool robe into her marriage, listed in her marriage contract. After her husband died, his orphaned children used the robe to cover his body as a shroud, and she demanded it back. Rava ruled that the dead man had acquired it, and it is forbidden to benefit from something set aside for the dead. When challenged with another ruling, Rav Kahana answered that the robe had not yet been collected by the woman, so it still belonged to the husband's estate and his heirs could make it a shroud.

people.name: Rava
people.about: ruled the robe was acquired by the dead man

people.name: Nanai, son of Rav Yosef, son of Rava
people.about: raised the objection

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: answered the objection

terms.meaning: Property a wife brings into marriage that the husband takes responsibility for, and must pay back its value.
A cloth wrapped around or spread over a dead body for burial.

yevamot-66b-7-8.why: The discussion is about who owns property a wife brings into marriage at a fixed value: Rav Yehuda says she may take it back as a family heirloom. This case tests that view, and the Gemara links Rava's ruling to his rule that consecrating something frees it from a debt claim.

yevamot-72b-3-6.note: Rabbi Yochanan taught that notar, leftover sacrificial meat that must be burned, is burned only by day when burned at its proper time. Rabbi Elazar objected with a baraita about circumcision, which reads the word 'and' in a verse as extending the rule to other cases, and said the same hint appears for notar. Rabbi Yochanan had no answer. Afterward he told Reish Lakish how impressive this was, and Reish Lakish said it is a baraita found in Torat Kohanim. Rabbi Yochanan then learned the whole book in three days.

people.name: Rabbi Yochanan
people.about: was teaching

people.name: Rabbi Elazar, son of Pedat
people.about: raised the objection

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: told Rabbi Yochanan the source

terms.meaning: Meat of an offering left over past its allowed time, which must be burned.
A teaching from the time of the Mishnah that was not included in it.
An ancient commentary on the Book of Leviticus.

yevamot-72b-3-6.why: The Gemara has explained that two early Sages disagree over whether the word "and" in a verse makes a late circumcision a daytime-only act. This episode shows Rabbi Yohanan holding the same view about leftover sacrificial meat, and being challenged on it.

yevamot-75a-18-18.note: A man was climbing a palm tree when a thorn pierced his testicles, and a discharge like a thread of pus came out of him. Later he had children. Shmuel sent the case to Rav, who told him to go and find out where the man's children came from.
yevamot-75a-18-18.why: The discussion asks whether a man whose testicles were pierced counts as having crushed testicles, a condition that bars him from marrying into the community. The case seems to show such a man can father children, but Rav's reply suggests the children were not his.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage who sent the case to Rav.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage who doubted the children were the man's own.

terms.meaning: An injury the Torah lists as barring a man from marrying a Jewish woman by birth ("entering the congregation").

yevamot-75b-15-15.note: In Mata Mehasya a man's member had been cut like an open gutter; Mar bar Rav Ashi trimmed it into the shape of a quill and declared him fit. In Pumbedita a man's seminal duct became blocked and he emitted semen through the urinary duct. Rav Beivai bar Abaye wanted to declare him fit. Rav Pappi mocked him, saying that coming from a short-lived family he spoke short-lived words, since semen that does not pass through its proper place does not fertilize.
yevamot-75b-15-15.why: The discussion is about which injuries to the genitals bar a man from marrying into the community. Rav Pappa has just ruled that a cut shaped like a quill or a gutter is fit, and these cases apply that ruling and test where it stops.

people.name: Mar bar Rav Ashi
people.about: Reshaped an injured man's member and declared him fit.

people.name: Rav Beivai bar Abaye
people.about: Wanted to declare the Pumbedita man fit.

people.name: Rav Pappi
people.about: Mocked Rav Beivai's ruling and held the man unfit.

terms.meaning: Permitted to marry a Jewish woman by birth ("enter the congregation"), despite the injury.
Rav Pappi's insult: Rav Beivai's family was descended from the priest Eli, whose descendants were cursed to die young.

yevamot-77b-8-9.note: When Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda came from the Land of Israel, he reported that Rabbi Zakkai once recited a baraita before Rabbi Yoḥanan: an Ammonite woman is fit, her son from an Ammonite man is unfit, and her daughter is fit, but only when both parents converted; her daughter from an Ammonite married to a Jewish woman is unfit. Rabbi Yoḥanan told him: Go out and teach it outside. He took the teaching apart line by line, showing which parts were obvious, and rejected the last line.
yevamot-77b-8-9.why: Rav Yosef has just supported Rabbi Yoḥanan's view that the daughter of an Ammonite convert and a Jewish woman may marry a priest; this report shows Rabbi Yoḥanan dismissing a baraita that says otherwise.

people.name: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who brings this report from the Land of Israel

people.name: Rabbi Zakkai
people.about: The Sage who recites the baraita

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: The Sage who rejects the baraita

terms.meaning: A member of a nation the Torah bars from marrying into Israel; the Sages apply the ban to men only.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.

terms.term: Go out and teach it outside
terms.meaning: A dismissal: this teaching is unreliable and should not be studied in the study hall.
Families of priests descended from Aaron, who may marry only women of qualifying lineage.

yevamot-78a-12-12.note: Rabbi Yehuda recalls his friend Minyamin, an Egyptian convert who studied with Rabbi Akiva. Minyamin said that he, a first-generation Egyptian convert, had married another first-generation Egyptian convert, and that he planned to marry off his son to a second-generation Egyptian convert so that his grandson would be allowed to enter the congregation. The Gemara adds that Rabbi Yohanan told the teacher reciting this account to change it: Minyamin meant to marry his son to a first-generation convert.
yevamot-78a-12-12.why: The Gemara is asking whether a child's generation is counted from the father or the mother. Rava uses Minyamin's plan to challenge the view, credited to Rabbi Yohanan, that the father decides; the corrected wording answers him.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who reports what his friend Minyamin told him.

people.name: Minyamin
people.about: An Egyptian convert, a friend of Rabbi Yehuda and a student of Rabbi Akiva, planning whom his son should marry.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who cites this account as an objection.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A Sage who told the reciter to correct the wording of the account.

terms.meaning: The Torah says Egyptians who join the Jewish people may marry into the community only from the third generation. A first- or second-generation Egyptian convert may not marry a born Jew.
To be allowed to marry a born Jew.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.
Here, a person whose job was to memorize and recite early teachings word for word.

yevamot-78b-11-11.note: Rabbi Ami investigated a man in his neighborhood and declared him a mamzer, a person born from a forbidden union who is barred from marrying most Jews. The man went around weeping. Rabbi Ami told him not to be upset, because by making it publicly known he had given him life. The text says that once someone is publicly known as a mamzer, he and his descendants may survive.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: declared the man a mamzer

terms.meaning: A person born from certain forbidden unions, who is barred from marrying most Jews.

yevamot-78b-11-11.why: The Gemara has just quoted Rav Yehuda that a mamzer who is publicly known survives, while one who is not known dies at the hand of Heaven. Rabbi Ami's words to the weeping man apply that teaching.

yevamot-84a-2-2.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi recalls going to learn Torah from Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua. The students there ganged up on him like the fighting roosters of Beit Bukya and would not let him study. He managed to learn only one thing: Rabbi Eliezer's ruling that a man who has intercourse with a hermaphrodite is liable to stoning, as if with a male.
yevamot-84a-2-2.why: The mishna quotes Rabbi Eliezer's ruling about a hermaphrodite, and the Gemara has just shown that Rabbi Eliezer does not treat a hermaphrodite as a full male. This memory of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi confirms the wording of that ruling.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: A Sage, called simply Rabbi, who tells of his attempt to study with Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua
people.about: The teacher whose students would not let Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi learn.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: The Sage whose ruling on a hermaphrodite was the one thing Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi learned there.

terms.meaning: A person with both male and female sexual organs, whose legal status the Sages debate.
The severest form of court execution in Jewish law, prescribed for certain forbidden sexual acts, including relations between males.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.

yevamot-86b-2-2.note: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, a priest, took the first tithe from a certain garden, since he held that priests are also entitled to it. Rabbi Akiva closed the garden and moved its entrance to face a cemetery, which a priest may not enter, to keep him out. Rabbi Elazar joked about Akiva, the former shepherd, and asked where his own livelihood would come from. The text adds that he was in fact very rich and was making a point about being blocked from what he saw as his due.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
people.about: a priest

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: closed the garden and moved the entrance

terms.meaning: A tenth of the harvest given to the Levites; Rabbi Elazar held priests may take it too.
Priests are forbidden to enter burial places because of ritual impurity.

yevamot-86b-2-2.why: The Gemara has just set out the dispute: Rabbi Akiva holds the first tithe belongs only to Levites, Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya that a priest may receive it too. This episode shows each acting on his view; afterwards the Gemara asks why Rabbi Akiva blocked the entrance.

yevamot-90b-9-9.note: Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov taught that the court may sometimes punish where the Torah does not require it, to build a fence around the Torah. As an example, in the time of the Greeks a man rode a horse on Shabbat, which was forbidden only by rabbinic law. The court stoned him as a Shabbat violator, not because he deserved it, but because Jews at that time were careless about Shabbat and the hour demanded it.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov
people.about: told the incident

terms.meaning: A rabbinic rule or measure meant to keep people far from breaking a Torah law.

yevamot-90b-9-9.why: The Gemara is asking whether the Sages have the power to uproot a Torah law. This report of a court executing a man for an act the Torah does not punish by death is brought as evidence that they can.

yevamot-90b-10-10.note: A man had relations with his own wife under a fig tree, in public view. He was brought to court and flogged, not because he deserved it, but because the times required it.
yevamot-90b-10-10.why: The Gemara is asking whether the Sages can uproot a Torah law by an active deed. This second precedent, after the man stoned for riding on Shabbat, seems to say they can; the Gemara limits it to safeguarding the Torah.

terms.meaning: Given lashes, a punishment a court could impose.

yevamot-93a-7-8.note: Rabbi Yannai's sharecropper brought him a basket of fruit every Shabbat eve. One day he was late, so Rabbi Yannai separated tithes in advance for the fruit he expected, so as not to be unable to tithe on Shabbat. Unsure that this works for fruit not yet in hand, he asked Rabbi Chiyya, who said he had acted well and gave a source. Rabbi Yannai worried because a dream had shown him the words 'bruised reed.' Rabbi Chiyya said the dream referred to a verse about the Messiah, meaning he had acted rightly.

people.name: Rabbi Yannai
people.about: tithed in advance

people.name: Rabbi Chiyya
people.about: approved his act

terms.meaning: A portion of produce that must be set aside for priests, Levites, or the poor before the food may be eaten.
A farmer who works the owner's land and pays him part of the harvest.

yevamot-93a-7-8.why: The Gemara is listing Sages who hold that a person can act on something that does not yet exist or is not yet his. This episode is its proof that Rabbi Yannai, like Rabbi Hiyya, holds that view.

yevamot-95a-7-7.note: A man had relations with his mother-in-law. Rav Yehuda had him brought and flogged. Rav Yehuda told him: If Shmuel had not said that the law does not follow Rabbi Yehuda, I would make your wife forbidden to you for ever.
yevamot-95a-7-7.why: Rabbi Yehuda holds that a man who sleeps with his mother-in-law becomes forbidden to his wife, and Shmuel ruled against him. This case shows Rav Yehuda following Shmuel's ruling in practice.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who judged the man and reported Shmuel's ruling.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Rav Yehuda's teacher, who ruled that the law does not follow Rabbi Yehuda.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: An earlier Sage who held that such a man is forbidden to his wife.

terms.meaning: Jewish law; the binding ruling on a question.

yevamot-96b-13-17.note: Rabbi Elazar taught a law in the study hall without saying it came from his teacher, Rabbi Yohanan, who got angry. Two colleagues tried to calm him with a story about two sages whose angry dispute ended with a Torah scroll being torn as they pulled it between them, which only made him angrier. Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi then compared it to Joshua, who taught Moses' Torah without always naming Moses, and Yohanan was appeased. The text explains Yohanan cared because a teaching quoted in a scholar's name keeps his lips moving in the grave.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: the teacher who was angry

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: Yohanan's student, who taught without naming him

people.name: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi
people.about: two colleagues who tried and failed to calm him

people.name: Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi
people.about: the one who calmed him

terms.meaning: a point of Jewish law
a teaching from the time of the Mishnah that is not in the Mishnah itself

yevamot-96b-13-17.why: The ruling Rabbi Elazar repeated is the one just discussed, about a minor's relations with his yevama. The Gemara then explains Rabbi Yohanan's anger: a Sage quoted by name in this world, his lips move in the grave.

yevamot-98a-3-3.note: Rabbi Yosei reports a case: Niftayim, a convert, married the wife of his brother from the same mother. The case came before the Sages, who said that a convert has no marriage. The Gemara objects that a convert's marriage is surely valid, and rereads the ruling to mean that the ban on a brother's wife does not apply to a convert.
yevamot-98a-3-3.why: Rav Aha bar Yaakov and Rav Sheshet disagree over a convert and his maternal brother's wife. This case is offered as proof that it is permitted even if the brother married her after converting; the Gemara answers that he married her before.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The Sage who reports the case.

people.name: Niftayim
people.about: A convert who married the wife of his brother from the same mother.

terms.meaning: A person who has joined the Jewish people. In Jewish law a convert is like a newborn, so earlier family ties may not count.
The Torah forbids a man to marry his brother's wife, apart from the special case of levirate marriage.

yevamot-98a-5-5.note: Ben Yasiyan traveled to cities overseas and found a convert married to the wife of his brother from the same mother. He asked: My son, who allowed you this? The convert pointed to a woman and her seven sons and said that on this very bench Rabbi Akiva sat and taught two things: a convert may marry his maternal brother's wife, and God spoke to Jonah only twice, not a third time.
yevamot-98a-5-5.why: The Gemara is asking whether a convert may marry his maternal brother's wife even when the brother married her after converting. This account is offered as proof; the Gemara answers that the brother married her before converting, then asks whether the convert can be trusted.

people.name: Ben Yasiyan
people.about: A Sage who met the convert on his travels and questioned him.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: The Sage who, according to the convert, permitted this marriage.

people.name: Jonah
people.about: The biblical prophet, mentioned in the second teaching of Rabbi Akiva.

terms.meaning: A person who has joined the Jewish people. In Jewish law a convert is like a newborn, so earlier family ties may not count.
God's presence as it reveals itself to people, here in speaking to a prophet.
Coastal cities beyond the Land of Israel.

yevamot-99b-9-10.note: Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok said he testified in court only once, and a slave was promoted to the status of a priest on his word, an error. The Gemara finds that hard to believe, since God does not let even the animals of the righteous cause a mishap. It restates that they only wanted to promote the slave: Rabbi Elazar saw a man receiving teruma in one town and testified in another, not realizing this would be taken as proof the man was a priest.

terms.meaning: A portion of the harvest given to priests, which only priests may eat.
A teaching from the time of the Mishnah that was not included in it.

yevamot-99b-9-10.why: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei disagree on whether teruma may be handed to a priest's slave without his master, because in Rabbi Yehuda's town receiving teruma was taken as proof of priestly lineage. This account shows what that local difference could lead to.

yevamot-101b-14-14.note: Rav Ashi came to Rav Kahana's house, and Rav Kahana asked him to come up and make a fifth judge for a halitza. Rav Kahana recalled that Rav Yehuda once told him to go up to the bundle of reeds and join the five. When people asked Rav Yehuda why five were needed, he said it was to make the matter public.
yevamot-101b-14-14.why: The Gemara has ruled that halitza needs only three judges, and that it takes place at a set location. These cases of five judges at a fixed spot explain why the Sages sometimes used more: to publicize it, not because the law requires it.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: A Sage visiting Rav Kahana, who was asked to make up the five.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: A Sage who invited Rav Ashi to join and recalled an earlier case with Rav Yehuda.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Rav Kahana's teacher, who used five judges for halitza to make it public.

terms.meaning: The ceremony that releases a childless widow from marrying her late husband's brother. She removes his shoe and spits before a court, and is then free to marry anyone.
A spot marked by a bundle of reeds, set aside as the regular place where the court met for halitza.

yevamot-101b-15-16.note: Rav Yehuda asked Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda to join the five men watching a halitza ceremony. Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda pointed out that the law requires a court of Jews who are Jews from birth, and he admitted he was a convert along with his father. Rav Yehuda praised his honesty, saying he would accept his word to cancel a debt document, and the Gemara clarifies that one man's word cannot collect money.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: asked him to join

people.name: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda
people.about: said he was a convert, so he could not serve

terms.meaning: a ceremony in which a widow removes her brother-in-law's shoe, freeing her to remarry

yevamot-101b-15-16.why: The discussion is about who may sit on a court for halitza. Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda's refusal leads the Gemara to Rava's rule on when a convert may judge, and to why a halitza judge needs two Jewish-born parents.

yevamot-102a-7-8.note: Rabbi Yosei tells of meeting an Elder in Netzivin who had seen Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira perform halitza many times. The Elder insisted the Torah's word for shoe means a hard sandal, not a soft leather shoe. Rabbi Yosei asked why, then, Rabbi Meir holds that halitza done with a soft shoe is valid after the fact. The Gemara adds that Rabbi Ya'akov, in Rabbi Meir's name, permits it even from the start, and then asks the reason of those who forbid it.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira
people.about: from Netzivin

terms.meaning: A ceremony in which a widow whose brother-in-law will not marry her removes his shoe, freeing her to remarry.
A childless widow connected to her late husband's brother.
From the start, as opposed to after the fact.

yevamot-102a-7-8.why: The Gemara has been asking whether halitza may be done with a soft leather shoe from the start, or is only valid after the fact. It cites this account to show that early Sages disagreed on it, then asks the reason of those who forbid it.

yevamot-103b-5-6.note: Abaye stood before Rav Yosef when a widow came for halitza, and Rav Yosef asked Abaye for his sandal for the ceremony. Abaye gave his left one, and Rav Yosef noted that a left shoe is only acceptable after the fact. Abaye replied that the same is true of a borrowed shoe, and Rav Yosef said that was his point: give the shoe as a temporary gift so it is truly his, making the ceremony ideal.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: gave his sandal

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: asked for it and set the rule

terms.meaning: a ceremony in which a widow removes her brother-in-law's shoe, freeing her to remarry
from the start, as the ideal way, as opposed to 'after the fact' when it is only acceptable

yevamot-103b-5-6.why: The mishna says halitza is valid with a shoe that is not the brother's own, and the Sages read "his shoe" as one that fits him. This episode shows that using a borrowed or left shoe is still not the ideal way.

yevamot-105a-5-7.note: A woman spat before taking off the brother-in-law's shoe, which is the wrong order for halitza, and Rabbi Ami said she need not spit again. Rabbi Abba bar Memel objected, but Rabbi Ami warned that repeating it could lead people to wrongly permit a woman who has already done halitza. Rabbi Abba thought he was dodging, but afterwards he checked and found a teaching that the ceremony counts either way.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: the judge who ruled

people.name: Rabbi Abba bar Memel
people.about: objected, then checked and agreed

terms.meaning: a ceremony in which a widow removes her brother-in-law's shoe, freeing her to remarry
a teaching from the time of the Mishnah that is not in the Mishnah itself

yevamot-105a-5-7.why: The Gemara is weighing a ruling sent to Shmuel's father: a widow who spat first need only remove the shoe and need not spit again. This case is cited as an instance of that ruling.

yevamot-105a-8-9.note: Levi went to villages to teach Torah and was asked three questions he could not answer, so he asked at the house of study. They said an armless woman may perform halitza, since the Torah does not require using the hand, and that spitting blood still counts since the verse says only 'she shall spit'. A verse mentions 'writing of truth', suggesting some writing in Heaven is not true; the answer is that a judgment sealed with an oath cannot be canceled, while one without an oath can.

terms.meaning: A ceremony in which a widow whose brother-in-law will not marry her removes his shoe, freeing her to remarry.
A childless widow connected to her late husband's brother.

yevamot-105a-8-9.why: The Gemara has just told how Rabbi Abba bar Memel checked a halitza ruling in the study hall. Levi's questions bring more halitza cases, and his third question leads into the discussion of a decree sealed with an oath, shown by the house of Eli.

yevamot-105a-13-13.note: Rabba taught that a descendant of the house of Eli cannot gain atonement through sacrifice, but can through Torah study. Abaye taught that he can through acts of kindness. Both were themselves from the house of Eli: Rabba, who devoted himself to Torah, lived forty years, and Abaye, who devoted himself to Torah and kindness, lived sixty.
yevamot-105a-13-13.why: Rabbi Yonatan has just shown from the oath against Eli's house that a sentence sealed with an oath cannot be torn up, even with offerings. Rabba and Abaye read that verse as leaving another way out.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: A Sage descended from the house of Eli who devoted himself to Torah and lived forty years.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage descended from the house of Eli who devoted himself to Torah and kindness and lived sixty years.

terms.meaning: The descendants of Eli, the priest at Shiloh in the Book of Samuel. God swore that their sin would not be atoned for by sacrifice, and that they would die young.
Good deeds done for others, such as helping the needy, visiting the sick and burying the dead.
Animal and grain offerings brought at the Temple, among other things to atone for sin.

yevamot-105a-14-14.note: A Jerusalem family kept losing its children around age eighteen and went to Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai. He said they might descend from the house of Eli, whose descendants were told they would die as young men, and advised them to immerse themselves in Torah study. They did, lived longer lives, and were called the family of Yohanan.

people.name: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai
people.about: the sage who advised them

people.name: Eli
people.about: a biblical priest whose house was told its men would die young

terms.meaning: a teaching from the time of the Mishnah that is not in the Mishnah itself

yevamot-105a-14-14.why: The Gemara has just told how Rabba and Abaye, descendants of Eli, lived longer through Torah and kindness. This account from the Sages is a second example that Torah study can overcome the decree against Eli's house.

yevamot-105b-3-10.note: Rabbi Ḥiyya and Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi were debating whether one who prays should look down or up, each citing a verse. Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei, joined them and quoted his father: eyes down, heart up. When Rabbi entered the study hall, the heavy Rabbi Yishmael stepped over the heads of those seated, and Rabbi's attendant Abdon challenged him; the exchange ended with Yishmael asking, 'Is your teacher God?' When a yevama came, Rabbi sent Abdon to examine her, but Yishmael quoted his father that a minor may perform ḥalitza, so Rabbi called Abdon back. Yishmael rebuked him for stepping over heads again, and Rabbi told Abdon to stay where he was. At that moment Abdon was struck with leprosy, his two sons drowned, and their wives refused their marriages.
yevamot-105b-3-10.why: The Gemara asks who the Rabbis are who, against Rabbi Meir, let a female minor perform ḥalitza, and answers that it is Rabbi Yosei, as his son reports him in this incident.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: Sits debating the direction of one's gaze in prayer with Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: A very heavy Sage who quotes his father's rulings and clashes with Abdon.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, head of the study hall; Abdon is his student and attendant.

people.name: Abdon
people.about: Rabbi's student and attendant, who challenges Rabbi Yishmael and is then punished.

people.name: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak
people.about: Comments that God shamed Abdon in this world, sparing him in the World-to-Come.

terms.meaning: The ceremony in which a childless widow removes the shoe of her late husband's brother, releasing both from the duty of levirate marriage so she may marry someone else.
A childless widow bound to her late husband's brother under the law of levirate marriage until he marries her or performs ḥalitza.
A girl married off as a minor could annul the marriage by declaring that she refuses her husband.

yevamot-106a-3-3.note: A widow was bound to her late husband's brother, but he was not suitable for her. The judges told him to let her perform ḥalitza on condition that she pay him two hundred dinars. The case later came before Rabbi Ḥiyya, and he ruled that the ḥalitza was valid.
yevamot-106a-3-3.why: The Gemara is defining the 'mistaken ḥalitza' that the Sages call valid. Following Rabbi Yoḥanan it means a ḥalitza done on a condition of payment, and this incident is cited from a baraita in support.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: The Sage before whom the case came; he validated the ḥalitza.

terms.meaning: The ceremony in which a childless widow removes the shoe of her late husband's brother, freeing her to marry someone else.
The brother of a man who died childless, who is obligated either to marry the widow or to release her through ḥalitza.
A silver coin; two hundred dinars was a substantial sum.

yevamot-106a-4-5.note: A man brought his brother's widow to Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba so the court could press her to marry him. She told Rabbi Hiyya she knew the man was after her money and would not be good for her. Rabbi Hiyya told the man that she would remove his shoe as a form of marriage, which was really halitza, and it left her forbidden to him forever. He then asked the man to allow a second, proper halitza so she could marry others.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba
people.about: the sage who handled the case

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: his view is that a halitza done under a mistaken belief does not count

terms.meaning: a ceremony in which a widow removes her brother-in-law's shoe, freeing her to remarry
the brother-in-law and the childless widow tied to him

yevamot-106a-4-5.why: Reish Lakish defined a valid mistaken ḥalitza as telling the brother that ḥalitza would marry him, and Rabbi Yoḥanan rejected it. Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba uses exactly that ploy and then adds a proper second ḥalitza.

yevamot-106a-6-10.note: Rav Pappa's sister-in-law was tied to a brother-in-law who was not suitable, and Abaye had him do halitza on the condition that she pay two hundred dinars. After it was done, Rav Pappa argued she had only been fooling him, and cited a teaching about a prisoner promising a ferryman too much, so she owed nothing. Abaye agreed. Amazed at the young man's sharpness, Abaye asked about his parents and, envious that his own were not alive, looked on them, and both died.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: the judge who heard the case

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: a young man who argued on his sister-in-law's behalf

terms.meaning: a ceremony in which a widow removes her brother-in-law's shoe, freeing her to remarry
a teaching from the time of the Mishnah that is not in the Mishnah itself

yevamot-106a-6-10.why: The Gemara is discussing which mistaken ḥalitza counts. This case puts Rabbi Yoḥanan's version, ḥalitza on condition of payment, into practice and shows the woman need not actually pay.

yevamot-106b-7-8.note: Rav Ashi found Rav Kahana struggling to prompt a widow to recite 'He did not wish to consummate the levirate marriage' as one unbroken phrase. Rav Ashi asked whether he did not hold Rava's view that such a pause does not matter. Rav Kahana answered that Rava concedes in the case of this phrase, and quoted Abaye's wording for the bill of ḥalitza, recording which verses she and the brother were each prompted to recite.
yevamot-106b-7-8.why: Abaye said the prompter must not split 'He did not' from 'wish to consummate', and Rava called such a split a mere pause. This exchange marks where Rava's leniency stops.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Questions Rav Kahana's insistence on an unbroken recitation.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: Prompts the widow at a ḥalitza ceremony and defends his care.

terms.meaning: The biblical duty of a man to marry the widow of his brother who died childless, unless he releases her through the shoe-removal ceremony of ḥalitza.
A document the court writes recording that the ḥalitza ceremony took place, so the widow can prove she is free to remarry.

yevamot-108a-7-7.note: The daughters-in-law of Abdan rebelled against their husbands, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi sent two Sages to look into it. When some women said to the daughters-in-law, Look, your husbands are coming, they answered: Let them be your husbands. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi said: There is no greater refusal than this.
yevamot-108a-7-7.why: The Gemara is asking whether something other than a formal refusal can end a minor's marriage, even after full marriage; it brings this case, argues the women may only have been betrothed, and still rules with Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira.

people.name: Abdan
people.about: The man whose daughters-in-law rebel against their husbands

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: The leader of the Sages who sends two Sages and rules on the case

terms.meaning: A girl married off as a minor by her mother or brother could leave the marriage by declaring she refuses her husband, without a divorce.
Jewish marriage had two stages: betrothal, which already binds the couple, and full marriage, when they begin living together.

yevamot-108b-10-11.note: In a time of danger a ruling was needed: may a girl who left her first husband by a bill of divorce, and her second by refusal, return to the first? Those involved hired a man for four hundred dinars to carry the question. He asked Rabbi Akiva, who was in prison, and he forbade it; he asked Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira in Netzivin, and he forbade it too. Rav Yehuda, quoting Rav, reads this into the verse 'We have drunk our water for money.'
yevamot-108b-10-11.why: The Gemara asks which early Sage holds that a minor's refusal of a later husband does not undo an earlier divorce. Rav's report names Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Asked the question while in prison and ruled it forbidden.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira
people.about: Asked the question in Netzivin and also ruled it forbidden.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Tells the incident in Rav's name.

terms.meaning: A girl married off as a minor could annul the marriage by declaring that she refuses her husband, without a bill of divorce.
The document (get) a husband gives his wife to end a marriage.
A period of persecution when teaching and asking about Jewish law was itself dangerous.

yevamot-108b-14-14.note: In a time of Roman persecution, a question had to be sent to the Sages. Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei says it concerned a girl who, as a minor, married a man's maternal uncle, and then married that man's paternal brother, who died: could she now refuse her first marriage, undoing it, so that her co-wife could marry the man in levirate marriage? Those involved hired two men for four hundred dinars, who asked Rabbi Akiva in prison and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira in Netzivin. Both forbade it.
yevamot-108b-14-14.why: The Gemara is identifying which Sages stand behind the mishna's rules on a minor who left one husband by divorce and another by refusal; Rav cited this episode, and Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei corrects which question was asked.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The Sage who says what question was really asked

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage held in a Roman prison, who forbids it

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira
people.about: A Sage in Netzivin, who also forbids it

terms.meaning: A girl married off as a minor could leave the marriage by declaring she refuses her husband, which undoes it.
When a man dies childless, his brother may marry his widow, or one of his widows if he had several.
Another wife of the same husband.
A relative one may not marry by rabbinic law, beyond the Torah's own list.

yevamot-110a-4-6.note: In Neresh a girl betrothed as a minor came of age and was seated in the bridal chair under the canopy before the marriage was consummated, but another man snatched her and married her. Rav's students did not require the second man to give her a divorce document. Rav Pappa says the first husband had already consummated the marriage; Rav Ashi says the snatcher acted wrongly, so the Sages cancelled his betrothal, even if done by intercourse, which they treated as a licentious act.

people.name: Rav Bruna and Rav Hananel
people.about: students of Rav who were there

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: gave one explanation

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: gave another

people.name: Ravina
people.about: asked Rav Ashi a follow-up question

terms.meaning: the first stage of marriage, which makes the woman legally bound to the man
the document that ends a marriage

yevamot-110a-4-6.why: The Gemara is testing Rav's view that a minor's betrothal holds once she grows up only if her husband then has intercourse with her. This incident, judged by his own students, seems to contradict it.

yevamot-113b-15-15.note: Rav Yitzhak bar Bisna lost the keys to the study hall, so people could not get in on Shabbat, and carrying a key in the public area is forbidden. Rabbi Pedat told him to lead children to where the keys were lost, and if they find them they will bring them on their own. The Gemara discusses whether this shows one need not stop a child from doing a forbidden act, and Abaye rejects the proof offered, noting that perhaps one must stop a child from breaking a Torah prohibition.

terms.meaning: An in-between area that is not fully public or private; carrying there is forbidden only by Rabbinic rule.

yevamot-113b-15-15.why: The incident opens a discussion of whether adults must stop a child from breaking a prohibition, which the Gemara goes on to test against other teachings.

yevamot-115a-3-3.note: At the end of a wedding, a fire broke out in the bridal chamber and the bride screamed 'Look at my husband!' People found an unrecognizable burned body and a hand lying nearby. Rav Hiyya bar Avin thought her claim could not be trusted, like cases where someone says a house was set on fire. Rava answered that those women never said 'look at my husband', and here the burned body and hand support her claim.
yevamot-115a-3-3.why: The Gemara is asking when a woman who reports her husband's death in a disaster is believed; it has just said a woman who survives a house fire is not, since he too may have been saved.

yevamot-115a-7-7.note: Rabbi Akiva recounts that when he went down to Neharde'a to intercalate the year, he met Neḥemya of Beit D'li. Neḥemya said he had heard that in Eretz Yisrael only Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava lets a woman remarry on the word of one witness, and Akiva confirmed it. Neḥemya told him: say to them in my name, you know this country is riddled with troops, that I received from Rabban Gamliel the Elder that a woman may marry on the word of one witness.
yevamot-115a-7-7.why: The Gemara asks whether one witness to a husband's death is believed in wartime. Rami bar Ḥama cites this account, and the debate turns on what Neḥemya's remark about troops means.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Tells of his meeting with Neḥemya.

people.name: Neḥemya of Beit D'li
people.about: A Sage in Neharde'a who passes on a tradition from Rabban Gamliel the Elder.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava
people.about: Said to be the only Sage in Eretz Yisrael relying on one witness.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel the Elder
people.about: The source of Neḥemya's tradition.

people.name: Rami bar Ḥama
people.about: Brings this account into the discussion.

terms.meaning: To add a leap month to the Jewish calendar so the festivals stay in their seasons, a decision made by the Sages.
The Land of Israel.

yevamot-115a-10-10.note: Two Torah scholars were traveling by boat with Abba Yosei ben Simai, and the boat sank. Rabbi allowed their wives to remarry on the testimony of women.
yevamot-115a-10-10.why: The Gemara asks whether one witness to a death is believed in wartime. Water is treated like war, and many women count as one witness, so this seems to say yes; the Gemara answers that the women gave identifying marks.

people.name: Abba Yosei ben Simai
people.about: Was traveling on the boat with the two scholars.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who allowed the widows to remarry.

yevamot-115b-7-7.note: Yitzḥak the Exilarch, son of Rav Beivai's sister, was traveling from Cortva to Spain and died. A message came from Spain reporting his death by name. The question was whether to worry that there were two men named Yitzḥak. Abaye said we are concerned; Rava said we are not. The text does not give the outcome.
yevamot-115b-7-7.why: The Gemara has just debated whether a labelled container may hold something other than its label says; the same doubt is now asked of a name, and Abaye and Rava go on to defend their views with other cases.

people.name: Yitzḥak the Exilarch
people.about: The man reported dead on the road to Spain.

people.name: Rav Beivai
people.about: Yitzḥak's uncle; Yitzḥak is his sister's son.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Holds we must worry about another man of the same name.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Holds we need not worry about that.

terms.meaning: The title of the head of the Jewish community in Babylonia.

yevamot-116b-9-9.note: At the end of the wheat harvest, ten people went out to harvest and a snake bit one, who died. His wife told the court he had died, and messengers found it was as she said. The sages then ruled that a woman who says her husband died may remarry on that basis. If he left no children and has a brother, she enters levirate marriage. This is the case Beit Hillel referred to.

terms.meaning: The duty of a childless man's brother to marry his widow.
The school of Hillel, whose opinions are often compared with Beit Shammai.

yevamot-116b-9-9.why: Beit Hillel hold that a woman's word about her husband's death is accepted only in circumstances like the original incident, Beit Shammai that it extends further; the Gemara asks what that incident was.

yevamot-116b-15-15.note: A person was carrying water and ashes of purification, made from the red heifer, across the Jordan River by boat. An olive-sized piece of a corpse was found stuck to the bottom of the boat, making the water and ashes ritually impure. In response the sages said that such things may not be carried on the Jordan River in a boat. The passage ends with a dispute over whether this applies to other similar cases or only this one.

terms.meaning: Ashes used with water to purify people who had contact with a corpse.
In a state that disqualifies something from holy use until purified.

yevamot-116b-15-15.why: Rabbi Ḥananya ben Akiva limits that decree to the Jordan and to boats, as in the incident, while the Rabbis apply it to all rivers; the Gemara compares this to the dispute of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel.

yevamot-120a-10-10.note: Abba bar Marta owed money to members of the Exilarch's household, who were known to be violent, and did not want to be seen by them. He stuck wax onto a strip of worn cloth and attached it to his forehead to change his look. He walked past them and they did not recognize him. The Gemara draws the lesson that changing the forehead changes a person's face a great deal.

people.name: Abba bar Marta
people.about: also called Abba bar Minyumi

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia.

yevamot-120a-10-10.why: A teaching just quoted says witnesses may identify a dead man only if they saw both his forehead and his face with the nose; this incident shows that changing the forehead alone can make a man unrecognizable.

yevamot-120b-7-7.note: In Asya, people lowered a man into the sea on a rope, and when they pulled it back only his leg came up in their hands. The Sages ruled that if the leg was cut off from the knee up, his wife may remarry; if from the knee down, she may not.
yevamot-120b-7-7.why: The Gemara proposed that the Mishna's rule against testifying about a man cut open follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, who says such a wound can heal. This incident treats a high cut as fatal and seems to contradict that; the Gemara answers that water aggravates a wound.

yevamot-121a-3-3.note: A man drowned at Carmi and was pulled out near Bei Hedya after three days, and Rav Dimi of Neharde'a allowed his wife to remarry. Another man drowned in the Tigris and was pulled out at the Bridge of Shabistana, and Rava allowed his wife to remarry on the testimony of his friends, five days after his death.
yevamot-121a-3-3.why: The Mishna allows identifying a body only within three days, and Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava disputes it; the Gemara asks whether he is more lenient or more strict. These rulings fit the lenient reading, but the Gemara answers that water keeps the body from changing.

people.name: Rav Dimi from Neharde'a
people.about: Allowed the first drowned man's wife to remarry.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Allowed the second drowned man's wife to remarry.

yevamot-121a-10-13.note: A man drowned in the lake at Samkei, and Rav Sheila let his wife remarry because witnesses saw him go in and not come out. Rav wanted to excommunicate Rav Sheila, but Shmuel suggested asking him first. Rav Sheila admitted he had erred: he thought the still water counted as having a visible edge, but waves could have carried the man out of sight. Shmuel and Rav then quoted verses praising each other's caution and advice.

people.name: Rav Sheila
people.about: the one who allowed the wife to remarry

terms.meaning: To formally ban someone from the community as punishment.
Water whose far edge cannot be seen; a man lost in it was not accepted as dead.

yevamot-121a-10-13.why: The Rabbis permit the wife only if the water has a visible end, and Abaye has just defined that as water whose shore can be seen on all four sides; this case shows a judge misapplying the rule.

yevamot-121a-14-14.note: Two men were fishing with nets on the Jordan River, and one went into a cave with a fish pond. Night fell and he could not find the opening, so his friend thought he had drowned and told his family. The next morning the man found the exit and came home to find people mourning him. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi said this shows how great the Sages' words are: a wife may remarry if her husband fell into water with a visible end, but not if it had no end.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: the sage who tells the incident

terms.meaning: A teaching from the time of the Mishnah that was not included in the Mishnah itself.

yevamot-121a-14-14.why: The discussion has just dealt with Rav Sheila, who let a wife remarry after her husband vanished in the lake of Samkei, then admitted his error because waves could carry a man out of sight. This incident shows why the Sages refuse to presume death when a man disappears in such water.

yevamot-121a-17-18.note: Rabban Gamliel saw a boat sink and grieved for the Torah scholar aboard, Rabbi Akiva. Later Akiva turned up on dry land teaching, and said a plank from the boat reached him and he bowed his head before each wave so none swept him off. From this the Sages said that if wicked people attack, one should bow his head and he will be saved. Gamliel said this showed how great the Sages' words are, that a wife may remarry if her husband fell into water with a visible edge but not with no edge.

terms.meaning: Jewish law.

yevamot-121a-17-18.why: The Gemara has just rejected Rav Ashi's idea that a Torah scholar's survival would surely become known, ruling that no one lost in endless water is presumed dead. This is one of several accounts of men seen lost at sea who came back alive.

yevamot-121a-19-19.note: Rabbi Akiva saw a boat sink and grieved for the Torah scholar aboard, Rabbi Meir. When Akiva landed in Cappadocia, Meir came and discussed law with him. Meir said one wave carried him to the next until one threw him onto dry land. Akiva said this showed how great the Sages' words are, that a wife may remarry if her husband fell into water with a visible edge but not with no edge.

terms.meaning: Jewish law.

yevamot-121a-19-19.why: This follows Rabban Gamliel's account of Rabbi Akiva surviving a shipwreck, as a second case of a man seen lost at sea who came back alive, backing the rule that a wife may not remarry when her husband vanished in endless water.

yevamot-121b-5-6.note: The daughter of Nehunya the well digger fell into a large cistern, and people asked Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa to pray for her. After the first and second hours he told them she was safe, and after the third that she had come out of the cistern. She said a ram and an old man leading it pulled her out. Asked if he was a prophet, he said no, and explained that he reasoned God would not let the righteous Nehunya's own child be harmed by his public service.

people.name: Nehunya the well digger
people.about: a righteous man who dug wells for the public

people.name: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa
people.about: a sage known for his prayers
